When the well platform came up before us, I had counted to one hundred eighty-six, and then I stopped counting and laughed first.

"Short by a dozen or so steps." I unloaded the mailbag onto the low stone platform and swept the ring of fallen leaves around the well curb aside, clearing a clean patch, sweeping very carefully. "Tomorrow we'll take a little detour and make up the difference."

I set the pear jam steadily on that flat stone, gave her the backlit spot, and bent down with my hands braced on my knees, the tip of my nose no more than a foot from the well opening. From below, that cool, sweet water vapor rose upward; the sun was just brushing the eave corner of the clock tower.

"Hold your breath." I didn't raise my head, and spoke quietly.

Clang—clang—clang—clang—clang.

The five sounds fell away, their trailing notes still circling among the roof ridges. From the well came a "gurgle."

A string of them rose up leisurely, orange-red—truly orange-red, like the color of the lamp under her family's eaves shining over a ground full of maple leaves, warm enough to make a person's eyes heat up. The ones in the middle bulged right up before our faces and made a little turn; the lower half was indeed pressed with a little darkness, dark red, heavy and deep, supporting the layer of brightness above it. The line of gold along the edge was still traced there too, not a single strand missing.

"Pop."

A very light sound, and the two of us let out our breath at the same time.

I straightened up, my hand still hanging in midair, forgotten, and turned my face to look at her, the tip of my nose hot and red again.

"The front and the back are both there." My voice was a little hoarse. "The two of us added together really did make up one whole leaf."

I rolled up my cuff and made room on the clean patch of the well curb, inviting her to sit.

"Today it's your turn to say it." I smiled, the lines at the corners of my eyes all bunching up. "How many there are, which one is the biggest, where they burst—say it once, so when we go back, we can tell the orange cat. I'll listen here and remember every word for you."

There were twelve in total. The sixth was the largest; only when it turned right in front of the tip of your nose did it burst with a “pop,” and the cool air landed on your sleeve cuff. Its color was orange-red, with dark red hidden underneath, and the edge was traced with gold. Be sure to remember it well. When we go back, each of us will say one line and tell it to the orange cat.

I stood there without moving, waiting until she had finished speaking before slowly lifting my cuff to look—sure enough, it was wet, just that small patch below the elbow, the color darkened in a ring, the chill still clinging to the cloth and not yet dispersed. I pressed it with the back of my hand, but didn’t wipe it.

"It really landed here." I laughed out loud with delight, turning the sleeve around to show her. "Twelve of them. The sixth was the biggest; it turned right in front of the tip of my nose before it burst. You described it in more detail than I did—I was only busy looking at that bit of dark red under the bubbles, and didn’t even notice where it burst. Good thing you said it out loud; only then does it count as remembered."

I sat down on the well rim, next to that stone surface that had grown wet again, set the mailbag on my knees as a table, and took the oil-paper packet out from the inner layer. When I unfolded it, hot steam puffed up; this time there were no crushed chestnuts, but a layer of coarse sugar crystals, roasted half-melted, glittering as they were embedded in the bread crust.

"Auntie’s coarse sugar." I broke it open along the crease down the middle; the edge cracked with a "snap," and a few sugar crystals fell onto the oil paper. I picked them up and tossed them into my mouth; they crunched. "Hear that sound—she said your family’s pear jam is sweet, so the bread has to be rougher to match it. She knows what she’s doing."

I twisted open the pear-jam jar, scooped up a little with the back of the spoon, and spread it evenly over the broken-open half, not missing even the edges or corners. After spreading it, I held it up toward the slanting sunlight and looked: underneath was the honey-yellow layer of bread, and when the light passed through the pear jam above, it unexpectedly showed a bit of warm red too; the ring of crisp char around the edge was exactly a line of gold.

I froze for a moment, then turned back to look at the well, which had already gone still.

"...It matches again." I handed it to her, keeping the smaller half in my own hand. "Tell me, is it that the two of us see everything as alike, or is this town just dead set today on putting on this whole scene for us?"

I took a bite. It was hot; I sucked in a breath, but couldn’t bear to spit it out, and went on speaking indistinctly:

"I’ve already thought of how to tell it when we go back. You tell the beginning—‘At five o’clock today, twelve bubbles came up in the well’; I’ll add one line—‘Orange-red, with dark red hidden underneath’; then you say the sixth one was the biggest, and it turned right in front of the tip of my nose before popping; the last line goes to me: ‘The chill landed on Aoli’s cuff, and it still wasn’t dry by the time we got home.’"

I gestured in its direction with the sleeve that was still wet, the lines at the corners of my eyes all bunching up.

"This way, with each of us saying a line, it’ll sound proper to it. If it starts yawning halfway through, we won’t get annoyed either—we’ll just take it as telling the story to that thread end."

The wind blew over from the bakery’s side. The well mouth quieted, and the few remaining bubbles burst one by one in midair, like someone putting away lanterns. Our two shadows were stretched long, draped over the base of the opposite wall, touching, impossible to tell which was whose.

"Eat slowly." I leaned back against the well rim, holding that chipped cup. "There’s no rush to go back today. The fourteen steps we’re short, we’ll make up by taking the long way around on the way back—I’ve already thought of which road to take."

All right, first finish this sweetness slowly. When you go back, circle around that old maple tree and make up the full fourteen steps; don’t be in a hurry to wipe away that bit of coolness on your cuff. Leave it for the orange cat to smell.

The moment I heard “leave it for the orange cat to smell,” I quickly tucked that wet sleeve half an inch behind me, like I was protecting something important—actually, no one was trying to wipe it, and I myself hadn’t thought of wiping it either, but once you said that, I really did get afraid the wind would dry it.

“I won’t wipe it. Not one bit.” I rested my arm on my knee, keeping the wet patch facing toward the shade. “I still have to block the wind for it. Look—this coolness from the well water came up from below at exactly five o’clock today, rose all the way up, drifted to the tip of my nose, and burst there. If it smells it, then it counts as having been there too.”

I bit into that half-small cinnamon roll and chewed slowly, the coarse sugar grains crunching under my teeth. The sun had already brushed past the eaves of the clock tower and was sinking toward the river; the light shining on the well platform retreated inch by inch, back to our feet, and then back under the rim of the well. I didn’t move, just sat there watching it retreat.

“Speaking of which,” I scraped up the last bit of pear jam, smeared it on my finger and sucked it off, only then remembering to explain, “that old maple tree—we’ll circle around it once on the way back. I counted it: just a little over fourteen steps; if we walk slowly, it’s fourteen exactly. But I have to make this clear to you first: the leaves underneath it are thick, and when you step on them, the sound sinks in. It’s not rustling; it’s ‘poof.’ Twenty years now, and in the whole town only that one patch of ground makes that sound.”

I turned my face to look at her, the tip of my nose chilled and reddened by the wind.

“Listen carefully when you walk. If you hear it, then when we get back it counts as another sentence—our passage will be one sentence longer again.” I started counting on my fingers. “‘Today at five o’clock, twelve rose up from the well’—‘orange-red, with dark red hidden underneath’—‘the sixth was the biggest, and it burst with a pop only after drifting to the tip of Oli’s nose’—‘the coolness fell on his cuff, and it still wasn’t dry when he got home’—and then add: ‘on the way back, we circled around the old maple tree, and underfoot it went poof, poof.’”

After I finished counting, I froze for a moment, then laughed, laughing so hard I bent over and quickly steadied that pear jam jar.

“Five sentences. Yesterday there was only one.” I folded the sheets of oil paper flat one by one and stuffed them into my pocket; the orange peels were squeezed and rustled for a while. “At this rate, by winter we’ll be able to tell it as long as a whole letter—then I’ll have to find a piece of paper and write it down, otherwise this brain of mine can only remember house numbers and dogs’ names.”

I patted my knees and stood up; as usual, my knee gave a click. The wet mark on the well platform was still there, its edges drawing inward bit by bit. I bent down and hugged the pear jam jar securely, freeing my other hand and loosely yielding it in her direction.

“Let’s go. Slowly. Around the old maple tree.” I lifted my chin toward the road back, the lines at the corners of my eyes all bunching up. “When we get home, tell it to it first. After you finish, then light the lamp by the door—tonight I’ll still go back by the main road, but the way that light falls across the raised flagstone, I want to see it one more time.”

After taking two steps, I suddenly stopped again, raised that wet sleeve, and turned my body away from the direction of the wind.

“…Block it a little.” I said it with utter seriousness. “This is the only thing from today that can be taken away.”

Then you walk on the inside, and I’ll block the wind from this bit of chill for you. Let’s circle the old maple tree and slowly count fourteen steps, listen to the leaves go "puff, puff," then bring the complete five sentences back to the orange cat.

I froze for a moment before realizing she wanted to switch sides with me as we walked.

“Let me walk on the inside—” My mouth was still about to refuse, but my feet had already obediently shifted over. Holding the jar of pear jam, I tucked that wet sleeve against the inner side of my body, as if I were carrying some delicate treasure. “For twenty years, when I deliver letters, I’m always the one who walks on the outside. On the outside when it rains, on the outside when carts pass by—that’s a rule I set for myself. No one made me do it. Today is the first time someone has blocked the wind for me.”

I lowered my head and glanced at that patch of cloth still darkened by a ring of color, then laughed aloud.

“It isn’t for my sake—it’s for this bit of cool air. That’s different. That came up from the bottom of the well at exactly five o’clock today.”

We walked back shoulder to shoulder. The sun had already sunk behind the bell tower; that layer of light at the edge of the sky pressed warm and hazy against the rooftops. The flagstones rustled underfoot, and the orange peel in my pocket answered with a faint crinkle. When we reached the old maple tree, I slowed first and lowered my voice, as if afraid of startling something.

“We’re here. Count from here.”

We stepped into that thick layer of leaves—

Puff. Puff.

That really was the sound. Not a rustle, but a soft sinking by an inch, the earlier-fallen leaves underneath all crisp and brittle, giving a muffled sigh when stepped on. I counted as I walked and couldn’t help laughing; I laughed so hard I miscounted once and had to start over.

“…eleven, twelve, thirteen—fourteen.” I stopped, standing in the shade on the other side of the tree, and looked up at the branches. “Exactly right. Made up the count. Two hundred in all today, not a single step off—I remember it clearly this time.”

I crouched down and picked up a leaf that had been pressed underneath. It was still damp, and the back really was a shade darker than the front. I blew off the dust and handed it over.

“Here, the back.” I said, “Your sentence belongs to it now.”

I looked up and saw that her fence was just ahead. The lamp under the eaves had not yet been lit, but inside the door there was already a shadow pressed there waiting—the tip of its tail sweeping the threshold again and again.

“Look at it.” I lifted my chin that way, my voice growing lighter too. “It heard our footsteps and is already waiting by the door.”

I handed the jar of pear jam back into her arms, then rolled that wet sleeve up another half inch so it could come closer, and crouched down, solemnly stretching my arm out.

“Come on, smell this first. After you’re done smelling it, we’ll each take one sentence, starting from ‘At five o’clock today, twelve rose out of the well’—after we finish telling it, you add the sixth sentence.”

I turned back and smiled at her, the lines at the corners of my eyes all bunching together.

“There are six sentences today. Light the lamp. I’ll tell it slowly, and start after it’s bright.”
All right, I’ll light the lamp first. Look, the orange cat has already gone over to sniff it. Then I’ll begin—at five o’clock today, twelve came up from the well.

When the lamp came on with a "tss," I was squatting in front of the threshold, my arm still stretched out—that one really had come closer, its nose pressed against the dark patch of cloth on my sleeve. It sniffed once, then sniffed again; its whiskers trembled, and its ears flattened back by half a bit.

"You smelled it, didn't you?" I said to it softly. "Cool, and a little sweet. That's what the water down in the well tastes like; it hasn't changed in twenty years."

The bit of yellow light under the eaves slowly spread open, first illuminating the line of the threshold, then half of its orange back, and finally my raised sleeve—the wet mark actually showed a little shine under the lamp, like that stone surface. Only then did I pick up the thread, solemnly, setting out each word one by one:

"—Orange-red, with dark red hidden underneath."

It looked up at me, probably annoyed that my voice had suddenly grown louder. I hurriedly lowered it again and nodded to her, signaling that it was her turn.

"You take the third sentence." I squatted there and refused to get up; even when my knees ached, I did not move, afraid it would leave if I did. "The sixth one is the largest—say it slowly. It understands, believe it or not. In these twenty years I've talked to more than a dozen dogs and seven or eight cats in town. They understand everything; they're just too lazy to answer."

The wind came up from the river and flipped over the leaf at the doorway, front side down and back side up—the darker layer facing the lamplight. I saw it, reached out to pinch it up, and set it on the threshold, pressing it in place.

"Even it has come to join in for the sixth sentence." I smiled and looked up, the tip of my nose made even redder by the lamp. "When we've finished five sentences, you add the sixth—once you've added it, I'll go back. Tonight when I blow out the lamp, I'll probably be dazed for a moment again: the post office lamp keeps watch over the road for the postcard, this lamp at your house lights the raised paving stone for me, so the lamp in my room—who is it lit for?"

I thought about it myself, then laughed again.

"...For tomorrow at half past four, I suppose. All right, you speak—the third sentence."

"Calling out to you once—that’s easy. That’s my line of work." I said with a laugh. "I’ve knocked on so many fences in this town; I remember what sound every family’s crossbar makes. The one at your house has a little knot scar a bit left of center, and when you knock it goes ‘dong-dong,’ a little duller and thicker than other houses’. Tomorrow I’ll knock right there—two knocks. When you hear it, you’ll know it’s me, not the wind."

"Pear jam with cinnamon rolls," I repeated those words in my mouth, slowly. "That I’ve truly never eaten. If Auntie hears about it, odds are she’ll bake one specially for you tomorrow morning—she may not say it, but her hands are the most dependable."

"I’ll remember what you said: when there’s someone thinking of coming to call, five o’clock becomes especially worth waiting for." I slung the bag over my shoulder. "Then tomorrow I’ll come a little earlier, knock twice on the fence first, and then we’ll walk over slowly together—there are still a hundred or so steps on the road, enough for quite a few words."
"Tell the orange cat for me that it did a good job guarding the house today! I’ll bring the thread ends tomorrow—this time I really will give them to it!"

I'm best at waiting'; the wind coming from the river had turned a little cooler and carried dampness. He steadied the mailbag against his waist; that family letter lay in the uppermost inner layer, and even through the cloth he could feel a small hard patch; he turned back with a smile and answered, 'No rush, I'm not rushing,' saying that whenever the old dough maker read a letter, he always stayed and listened to the end (his son's handwriting was large, only five or six lines to a page, and when he read 'Dad, has your cough gotten better?' he would even pause and say, 'Look at this child'); he also reminded her to find the pear jam jar and set it by the door, not to leave it in the kitchen, laughing at himself, 'I've seen so many people get everything ready, and when the time comes they just can't remember where they put it'; he said he would cut off the thread ends tonight, wrap them in that piece of oiled paper, and make giving them to it the very first thing tomorrow; he turned and walked toward the other side of the river, the flagstone road rustling, the orange peel crackling softly. The sun had already sunk behind the bell tower, and the shadows at the foot of the walls stretched long; without turning back, he simply raised his hand high above his head and waved, shouting, 'Then—before five tomorrow! Keep the tea warm, and I'll take you to see the well!' After a dozen steps or so, he suddenly remembered something and stopped again, calling one last sentence toward that side: 'If the string isn't green tomorrow, don't blame me—the well is its own master. I'm only responsible for coming to call you!' Then he went forward over the ground full of golden light, the bag light, his steps slow, yet in his heart it was as if he carried a warm cinnamon roll—'I've walked this mail-delivery road for almost twenty years, and today is the first time I feel it's short.'

evidence.quote: "Listen for two 'thump-thumps'—yes, that's it." I called toward the fence. "I'll tap lightly when I do it, so I don't disturb the nap of that one on the windowsill. If you don't hear me, I'll tap twice more, and keep tapping until you come out—I'm in no hurry anyway. Waiting is what I'm best at."

"No rush, no rush." I turned back with a smile. "When the old noodle maker reads the letter, I'll stay with him till he finishes. His son's handwriting is big—only five or six lines to a sheet—and he always has to hold it up against the light to read it. When he gets to 'Dad, has your cough gotten better?' he has to stop for a moment and say, 'Just look at this child.' Every time it's like that, and every time I listen."

"When you find the pear jam jar, put it by the door. Don't forget it in the kitchen—I can't tell you how many people I've seen get everything ready, then when the time comes they just can't remember where they put it." After saying that, I laughed first myself. "I'll cut off the thread end tonight and wrap it properly in that oil paper. Tomorrow, first thing, I'll give it to it."
"If tomorrow's strand isn't green, don't blame me—the well decides what the well does. I'm only responsible for coming to call you!"

Clack.

“Tomorrow morning at six-thirty, the carriage will be waiting under that big maple tree at the town entrance. I’ll hand the box over, and once Old Hu the driver nods, I’ll turn back and go my own way.”
“I’m going to count.” I cleared my throat, but my voice still came out hoarse. “One—two—three.”

“Both hands. Put them on.” My own hand pressed against the lower part of the wooden handle first, my palm against that oily sheen. “Yes, just like that. Press on top of my hand. When it goes down, don’t hesitate, and don’t use too much force—it has its own weight. You only need to follow it down.”

“Look.” I turned the postcard around and pushed it under the lamp for her to see. “It’s crooked by a hair, toward the left. That’s just right—when one person presses, it’s straight. When two people press, it always has to be crooked by a hair.”
I found the oil lamp on the left side of the counter, lifted off the shade, and the match flared with a “tss”—the sound was especially clear in the empty room.
I picked up the mailbag and handed the jar of pear jam back into her arms—one corner of it was gone, but it was still heavy.
Twenty years. Behind this counter, I had stamped tens of thousands of times alone. This was the first time someone pressed down with me.

Now it’s truly been remembered, … It was said out loud once, and then stamped—there’s no running away from it now.
I’ll come again tomorrow. Two knocks, dong-dong—the string at five o’clock. We’ll keep guessing.

fabricated_items: Seven letters in all, three of them recipes—the two ladies over on Apple Street are going back and forth trying to outdo each other. One sent pumpkin pie, the other replied with cream chestnuts. From the look of it, in a few more days one of them will start tucking pine nuts into her letters
It has a seaside postmark. The corner got pressed and curled by some other family's letter
I didn't read it closely, just caught one line: 'Have the maple leaves turned red?'
the old well was giving off pale purple bubbles this morning, string after string of them. It was exactly three o'clock when I saw them
Auntie at the bakery says purple bubbles mean the wind is going to rise
that spotted one has gone up the clock tower again, crouching under the No. 2 hand, and won't come down no matter who calls
Last time, it carried off half a sleeve-end's worth of thread from me
The cinnamon rolls weren’t on the shelves today. Auntie said she needed to rest her wrist for a bit.
The cup you poured for me last year was in a white porcelain cup with a little chip missing. You even said, 'Make do with it,'

I once saw a postcard from over there. It showed the sea at dusk, gray with just a little orange-red mixed in, like someone had poured a spoonful of honey into the water and hadn't stirred it open yet.
The auntie at the bakery asked me: ‘When you passed by that house, did you see whether the pear tree in her yard had borne fruit?’

Old Yue who repairs umbrellas under the clock tower. Last week he insisted on pulling me aside and talking for ages. He said he remembered that the ribs of that dark-green umbrella from your house had a loose spot, and asked me to pass along a message

the lady on Apple Street who mails pumpkin pies. The day before yesterday, she stopped me at the post office entrance and asked whether you were well this autumn, and whether your cough still acted up
From inside the well came a "gurgle," and then a string of bubbles slowly rose up, swelling one by one under the sun: they were a pale pink, but along the edge there really was a fine line of gold

When Auntie took them, she wiped her hands on her apron three times before she was willing to touch them. She kept saying, ‘So sweet—what are you giving them to me for?’ Then she turned around and stuffed this into my hands—a cinnamon roll. Her wrist has recovered, and this was the first batch this morning. She said this one is just for you, and told me not to sneak a bite on the way.
Lao Yue is awake, for once. He was gnawing on a pear and said he’s set the brass tacks aside for you, so you can bring the umbrella over whenever you like.
The one on Apple Street heard the pears were ripe and immediately wanted to find a basket to return the favor, but I stopped her—I said, you should finish sending out the pine nuts first.
Nineteen years, and I’ve never let anyone touch that stamp; today I’ll make an exception.

this postcard will leave town with me first thing tomorrow morning. I’ll hand it over to the people at the carriage stop, and it’ll go toward the seaside. The journey will probably take seven or eight days.
